intro: This topic follows a woman from the onset of labour to the end of the postnatal period: normal and abnormal labour, induction, operative birth, preterm labour and ruptured membranes, CTG interpretation, perineal trauma, the puerperium, breastfeeding, contraception and perinatal mental health. The AMC uses it to test safe intrapartum decisions (when to intervene, when to wait) and the postnatal problems a GP sees every week.

lessons.title: Normal labour and birth
objectives: Define the stages of labour and the expected rate of progress in each
Describe the mechanism of labour for an occipito-anterior position
Offer the options for pain relief and explain the trade-offs of an epidural
Conduct active management of the third stage and immediate newborn care

sections.heading: Birth in Australia
sections.body:
Around 300,000 women give birth in Australia each year, almost all in hospital, with a small number in birth centres or at home. About two-thirds of births are vaginal and just over a third are by caesarean section, a rate that has risen steadily. Midwives are the lead carers for normal labour; doctors are called for deviations from normal. As an intern you will be expected to recognise normal progress, know when to call for help, and not intervene without a reason.

Labour is the onset of **regular painful contractions** causing **progressive cervical effacement and dilatation**. Term is 37+0 to 41+6 weeks.

sections.heading: Stages of labour and expected progress
sections.body:
| Stage | From | To | Typical duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| First: latent phase | Onset of contractions | Active phase (around 5-6 cm; unit definitions vary) | Variable, can be many hours, especially in a first labour |
| First: active phase | Around 5-6 cm | **Full dilatation** (10 cm) | Progress of roughly 0.5-1 cm per hour or more |
| Second stage | Full dilatation | **Birth of the baby** | Passive (descent) then active pushing; limits commonly around 2-3 hours of pushing for a first labour, less for multiparous women, longer with an epidural (unit policy) |
| Third stage | Birth of the baby | **Delivery of the placenta** and membranes | Up to about 30 minutes with active management; up to about 60 minutes if physiological |

Progress is recorded on a **partogram**: cervical dilatation, descent of the head (in fifths palpable abdominally and station relative to the ischial spines), contractions (frequency per 10 minutes, duration, strength), maternal observations and fetal heart rate. A partogram makes slow progress visible early.

**Latent phase** care is usually at home with analgesia, fluids and reassurance, with clear advice on when to come in (regular strong contractions, ruptured membranes, bleeding, reduced movements, constant pain).

sections.heading: The mechanism of labour
sections.body:
The fetal head has to negotiate a pelvis whose widest diameter is transverse at the inlet and anteroposterior at the outlet. In the common **left occipito-anterior** position:

1. **Engagement**: the widest part of the head (biparietal diameter) passes the pelvic inlet; clinically, two-fifths or less palpable abdominally.
2. **Descent** throughout labour.
3. **Flexion**: presents the smallest diameter (suboccipitobregmatic, about 9.5 cm).
4. **Internal rotation**: the occiput rotates anteriorly to lie under the symphysis when it meets the pelvic floor.
5. **Extension**: the head is born by extending under the symphysis.
6. **Restitution**: the head untwists to realign with the shoulders.
7. **External rotation**: the shoulders rotate into the anteroposterior diameter.
8. **Expulsion**: anterior shoulder under the symphysis, then posterior shoulder and body.

**Occipito-posterior** position leads to a deflexed head presenting a larger diameter, backache, longer labour and more instrumental birth. Most rotate spontaneously.

sections.heading: Care in labour and pain relief
sections.body:
**Monitoring**: maternal pulse, BP and temperature, fluid balance and bladder care (a full bladder impedes descent and increases PPH risk). For **low-risk women**, the RANZCOG guideline recommends **intermittent auscultation** of the fetal heart (with a hand-held Doppler, listening after contractions, more often in the second stage). Continuous CTG is for women with risk factors (see the CTG lesson). An admission CTG is not recommended for low-risk women.

**GBS**: carriers (or at-risk women in risk-based units) receive **IV benzylpenicillin** from the start of labour or membrane rupture, ideally at least 4 hours before birth.

**Pain relief options**, from least to most invasive:

- Continuous support, mobilisation, water immersion, heat, massage, TENS, sterile water injections for back pain.
- **Nitrous oxide** and oxygen: quick on and off, can cause nausea.
- **Parenteral opioids** (morphine, fentanyl; pethidine is used less now): can cause maternal nausea and sedation and neonatal respiratory depression if given close to birth (naloxone should be available).
- **Epidural**: the most effective. It can cause hypotension, motor block, fever, urinary retention and itch, and it **lengthens the second stage and increases instrumental birth**, but it **does not increase caesarean section**. Rare: post-dural puncture headache, high block, local anaesthetic toxicity. Contraindications include coagulopathy, low platelets, local infection and uncorrected hypovolaemia.

sections.heading: The third stage and the first hour
sections.body:
**Signs of placental separation**: a gush of blood, **lengthening of the cord**, and the uterus becoming firm, globular and rising in the abdomen.

**Active management of the third stage** is recommended because it halves the risk of PPH:

1. **Oxytocin 10 IU IM** as the anterior shoulder is born or soon after birth.
2. **Delayed cord clamping** (at least 30-60 seconds in a vigorous baby), which improves infant iron stores and, in preterm babies, reduces the need for transfusion.
3. **Controlled cord traction** with counter-pressure above the symphysis once separated.

**Physiological third stage** (no uterotonic, maternal effort) is an informed choice for low-risk women, with conversion to active management if bleeding occurs or the placenta is not delivered within about an hour.

**Check the placenta and membranes** are complete (retained tissue causes PPH and infection), estimate blood loss, and examine the perineum.

**First hour**: skin-to-skin contact, early breastfeeding, and with consent, **vitamin K** IM and **hepatitis B vaccine** within 7 days (ideally in the first 24 hours). The Apgar score is recorded at 1 and 5 minutes.

sections.heading: Traps and discriminating clues
sections.body:
- Stages: first ends at full dilatation, second at birth of the baby, third at delivery of the placenta.
- Epidural lengthens the second stage and increases instrumental birth but **not caesarean section**.
- Low-risk woman in normal labour: **intermittent auscultation**, not continuous CTG.
- Active third stage uses **oxytocin**, not ergometrine, as the routine first choice.
- Head engaged means two-fifths or less palpable abdominally.
- Opioid given within a couple of hours of birth, floppy apnoeic baby: naloxone may be considered after ventilation is established.

keyPoints: First stage ends at full dilatation, second at birth, third at delivery of the placenta.
Active first stage usually starts around 5-6 cm; expect roughly 0.5-1 cm per hour or more.
A partogram tracks dilatation, descent, contractions and observations to show slow progress early.
Low-risk labour: intermittent auscultation; continuous CTG only for risk factors.
Epidurals lengthen the second stage and increase instrumental birth but not caesarean rates.
Active management of the third stage: oxytocin 10 IU IM, delayed cord clamping, controlled cord traction.
Always check the placenta and membranes are complete.
redFlags: Fresh vaginal bleeding in labour (abruption, praevia, vasa praevia)
Maternal fever in labour (chorioamnionitis)
Thick meconium-stained liquor
Constant abdominal pain between contractions

contrast.india: Admission CTG and frequent CTG strips are common in many hospitals.
contrast.australia: Intermittent auscultation for low-risk women per the RANZCOG guideline; no admission CTG.

quiz.stem:
A 27-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks is in spontaneous labour. At 08:00 the cervix was 5 cm dilated. It is now 12:00 and the cervix is 8 cm dilated, fully effaced, with the head at station 0 in an occipito-anterior position. She is contracting 4 times in 10 minutes. Intermittent auscultation is normal.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: Artificial rupture of membranes and oxytocin augmentation
Emergency caesarean section for slow progress
Continue supportive care and reassess progress in about 4 hours or earlier if indicated
quiz.explanation:
She is in the **active first stage** and has progressed 3 cm in 4 hours, about **0.75 cm per hour**. That is normal progress. The head is descending, the position is favourable and contractions are adequate. The fetal heart is normal on intermittent auscultation.

The right action is **continued supportive midwifery care**, with ongoing observations, bladder care and a vaginal examination at intervals (commonly about 4 hours, or sooner if there is a clinical reason).

Intervention (amniotomy, oxytocin, caesarean) is reserved for delay, and continuous CTG is for women with risk factors or abnormal auscultation. Unnecessary intervention in normal labour increases the chance of further intervention.
whyWrong: Augmentation is for delay; her progress is normal.
There is no delay or fetal compromise to justify caesarean.
Continuous CTG is not needed for a low-risk woman with normal auscultation.
Scalp sampling is only for an abnormal CTG; she has no indication.

quiz.stem:
A 30-year-old woman has a spontaneous vaginal birth of a healthy baby. She chose active management of the third stage. The baby is vigorous and skin-to-skin on her chest.

Which sequence best describes active management of the third stage?
options: Oxytocin 10 IU IM at or soon after birth, delayed cord clamping, then controlled cord traction after signs of separation
Ergometrine IV immediately, immediate cord clamping, then fundal pressure
Wait for spontaneous placental delivery for up to 60 minutes, then oxytocin if needed
Controlled cord traction immediately after birth before any uterotonic
Misoprostol orally, immediate cord clamping, then manual removal of the placenta
quiz.explanation:
**Active management of the third stage** reduces PPH and the need for transfusion. It consists of:

1. A **uterotonic**, **oxytocin 10 IU IM**, given with the birth of the anterior shoulder or soon after the baby is born.
2. **Delayed cord clamping** (at least 30-60 seconds in a well baby), which improves neonatal iron stores without increasing PPH.
3. **Controlled cord traction** with suprapubic counter-pressure once the uterus has contracted and signs of separation appear.

Ergometrine is not the routine choice because of hypertension and vomiting. Fundal pressure and traction before a contracted uterus risk **uterine inversion**. Waiting up to an hour describes a physiological third stage.
whyWrong: Ergometrine is not routine, immediate clamping is not preferred, and fundal pressure risks inversion.
This describes physiological management.
Traction before a uterotonic and a contracted uterus risks inversion.
Misoprostol is not first-line and manual removal is only for a retained placenta.

quiz.stem:
A 25-year-old primigravida in labour at 39 weeks asks about an epidural. She is worried it will mean she needs a caesarean section. Her platelets are 210 x 10^9/L and she has no medical problems.

Which statement about epidural analgesia is most accurate?
options: It increases the risk of caesarean section
It shortens the second stage of labour
It is contraindicated in first labours
It is associated with a longer second stage and more instrumental births but not more caesarean sections
quiz.explanation:
Epidural analgesia is the most effective form of labour pain relief. Large systematic reviews show it is associated with a **longer second stage** and a **higher rate of instrumental vaginal birth**, but **no increase in caesarean section**.

Other side effects include hypotension (preloading or vasopressors), maternal fever, itch, urinary retention needing catheterisation and reduced mobility. Rare complications include post-dural puncture headache, high block and local anaesthetic toxicity. It does **not** cause long-term backache.

Contraindications include coagulopathy, significant thrombocytopenia, anticoagulation, local sepsis and uncorrected hypovolaemia. None apply to her.
whyWrong: Evidence does not show an increased caesarean rate.
It lengthens rather than shortens the second stage.
First labour is not a contraindication.
Evidence does not support an association with long-term back pain.

lessons.title: Induction, slow progress and operative birth
objectives: Use the Bishop score to choose a method of induction
List the indications, contraindications and risks of induction of labour
Diagnose and manage delay in the first and second stage using the 3 Ps
State the prerequisites for instrumental birth and the categories of caesarean urgency
Counsel a woman about vaginal birth after caesarean

sections.heading: Why induction matters
sections.body:
Around a third of women in Australia have their labour induced, and the rate has risen. Induction is appropriate when the risks of continuing the pregnancy outweigh the risks of birth and induction, and the woman agrees after counselling.

**Common indications**:

- **Prolonged pregnancy**: offered from **41 weeks**, because stillbirth risk rises beyond term.
- **Prelabour rupture of membranes at term** (induction or expectant management for up to about 24 hours; induce promptly if GBS positive).
- Hypertensive disorders (pre-eclampsia at 37 weeks), diabetes, fetal growth restriction, reduced fetal movements with concerns, older maternal age, previous stillbirth, twins, intrauterine fetal death, and cholestasis.

**Contraindications** (any contraindication to vaginal birth): placenta praevia, vasa praevia, transverse lie, cord presentation, active genital herpes, previous classical caesarean or uterine rupture, and some fetal compromise needing immediate birth.

sections.heading: The Bishop score
sections.body:
The **Bishop score** assesses how favourable ("ripe") the cervix is, which predicts how likely induction is to succeed.

| Component | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dilatation (cm) | Closed | 1-2 | 3-4 | 5 or more |
| Length (cm) / effacement | More than 3 cm | About 2 cm | About 1 cm | Less than 1 cm |
| Station (relative to spines) | -3 | -2 | -1, 0 | +1, +2 |
| Consistency | Firm | Medium | Soft | |
| Position | Posterior | Mid | Anterior | |

A **score of about 6 or less** means an **unfavourable** cervix that needs ripening first. A **score of about 8 or more** is favourable, and labour can be induced with amniotomy and oxytocin.

sections.heading: Methods of induction and their risks
sections.body:
**Cervical ripening (unfavourable cervix)**:

- **Prostaglandin E2** (dinoprostone gel or controlled-release pessary) inserted vaginally. Risk: **uterine hyperstimulation** (tachysystole, more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes) with fetal heart changes. Generally avoided with a uterine scar.
- **Balloon catheter** (single or double balloon) through the cervix: mechanical dilatation, less hyperstimulation, and preferred for women with a **previous caesarean**. Some units use it for outpatient ripening.

**Favourable cervix**:

- **Amniotomy (artificial rupture of membranes, ARM)**: check the head is well applied to the cervix first, because a high head risks **cord prolapse**.
- **Oxytocin infusion**, titrated to contractions (about 3-4 in 10 minutes). Continuous CTG is required.

**Risks of induction**: hyperstimulation and fetal compromise, failed induction, longer labour, more epidurals and instrumental births, infection with prolonged membrane rupture, cord prolapse with ARM, and **uterine rupture** in women with a scar. Tachysystole is managed by stopping oxytocin or removing the pessary, and tocolysis (terbutaline) if the CTG is abnormal.

sections.heading: Slow progress: the 3 Ps
sections.body:
Delay is assessed separately for each stage.

**First stage**: progress slower than expected in the active phase (for example, less than about 2 cm in 4 hours) or descent and rotation not occurring. Causes:

- **Powers**: inadequate contractions, the commonest cause in a first labour. Treatment: **amniotomy** if membranes are intact, then **oxytocin augmentation**. Be very cautious with oxytocin in multiparous women, where slow progress is more likely to be obstruction, and in women with a scar.
- **Passenger**: malposition (occipito-posterior, deflexed), large baby, malpresentation (brow, face), fetal anomaly.
- **Passage**: cephalopelvic disproportion, a contracted pelvis, soft tissue obstruction.
- Also psyche: fear and exhaustion; and a full bladder.

**Signs of obstructed labour**: arrest of dilatation with increasing **caput and moulding**, a head that remains high, haematuria, maternal tachycardia and fever, a **Bandl's ring**, and fetal compromise. Oxytocin is dangerous here (rupture); the answer is **caesarean section**.

**Second stage delay**: consider the position, epidural, maternal exhaustion and the fetal condition. Options are oxytocin (in nulliparous women without obstruction), instrumental birth, or caesarean section if the head is too high or instrumental birth fails.

sections.heading: Operative birth and VBAC
sections.body:
**Instrumental birth (vacuum or forceps)** prerequisites, remembered as "**FORCEPS**":

- **F**ully dilated cervix
- **O**cciput position known (examine for fontanelles and sutures; ultrasound if unsure)
- **R**uptured membranes
- **C**ephalic presentation
- **E**ngaged head: no more than **one-fifth palpable abdominally**, at or below the ischial spines
- **P**ain relief adequate
- **S**phincter (bladder) empty
- Plus consent, an experienced operator and a plan to abandon if it is not progressing.

**Vacuum**: less maternal perineal trauma; more failure, cephalhaematoma, subgaleal haemorrhage and retinal haemorrhage; avoided before about 34 weeks and with face presentation. **Forceps**: more successful but more **third and fourth degree tears**; a **mediolateral episiotomy** is usually recommended with forceps (and considered with vacuum) because it reduces anal sphincter injury.

**Caesarean section urgency** (RANZCOG classification):

| Category | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Immediate threat** to the life of the woman or fetus | Cord prolapse, prolonged bradycardia, uterine rupture; aim for birth as soon as possible, often within 30 minutes |
| 2 | Maternal or fetal compromise, **not immediately life-threatening** | Failure to progress with some CTG concerns |
| 3 | Needs early birth, **no compromise** | Labour in a woman booked for elective caesarean |
| 4 | Elective, timed to suit | Planned repeat caesarean at 39 weeks |

Planned caesareans are usually at **39 weeks** to reduce neonatal respiratory problems.

**Vaginal birth after caesarean (VBAC)**: after one previous lower segment caesarean, planned VBAC succeeds in about 60-80% (higher if she has had a vaginal birth before). The main risk is **uterine rupture**, about 1 in 200, higher with induction or augmentation. Labour should be in hospital with **continuous CTG**, IV access and immediate access to theatre. **Contraindications**: previous classical or T-shaped incision, previous uterine rupture, placenta praevia. Elective repeat caesarean avoids labour risks but increases risks of placenta praevia and accreta in future pregnancies. It is a **shared decision**.

sections.heading: Traps and discriminating clues
sections.body:
- Bishop score 4 at 41+3 weeks: **cervical ripening** first (prostaglandin or balloon), not ARM.
- Previous caesarean needing induction: **balloon catheter** preferred over prostaglandin.
- Multiparous woman with slow progress: think **obstruction or malposition** before oxytocin.
- Head two-fifths palpable at full dilatation: **not** suitable for instrumental birth; caesarean.
- Cord prolapse is a category 1 caesarean; labour in a woman booked for elective caesarean is category 3.
- VBAC: success about 60-80%, rupture about 1 in 200; continuous CTG in labour.

keyPoints: Offer induction from 41 weeks for prolonged pregnancy.
Bishop score about 6 or less is unfavourable and needs ripening; 8 or more is favourable.
Prostaglandins can cause hyperstimulation; balloon catheters are preferred with a uterine scar.
Slow progress: think powers, passenger and passage; oxytocin fixes weak powers, not obstruction.
Instrumental birth requires full dilatation, known position, ruptured membranes and a head no more than one-fifth palpable.
Caesarean category 1 is an immediate threat to life; category 4 is elective.
VBAC succeeds in about 60-80%; uterine rupture risk about 1 in 200.
redFlags: Uterine tachysystole with an abnormal CTG during induction
Increasing caput and moulding with arrest of progress (obstruction)
Scar pain, bleeding or loss of station during VBAC
Haematuria and maternal tachycardia in prolonged labour

contrast.india: Repeat caesarean is often the default, especially in private hospitals.
contrast.australia: Planned VBAC is discussed and offered where suitable, with continuous CTG and theatre access.

contrast.india: Routine episiotomy in first vaginal births is still common in many units.
contrast.australia: Restrictive use; mediolateral episiotomy recommended with forceps and considered with vacuum.

quiz.stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida at 41+3 weeks attends for induction of labour. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. On vaginal examination the cervix is closed, 3 cm long, firm and posterior, with the head at station -3. The CTG is normal.

What is the most appropriate method to start the induction?
options: Vaginal prostaglandin E2 or a cervical balloon catheter
Membrane sweep and discharge home for 2 weeks
quiz.explanation:
Her **Bishop score is 0**: closed, long, firm, posterior cervix with a high head. An unfavourable cervix (score about 6 or less) needs **cervical ripening** before labour can be induced.

Options are **vaginal prostaglandin E2** (gel or pessary) or a **balloon catheter**. Once the cervix is favourable, amniotomy and oxytocin follow.

Amniotomy is not technically possible with a closed cervix and would risk cord prolapse with a high head. Oxytocin on an unripe cervix has a high failure rate. A membrane sweep is reasonable as an adjunct but sending her home for 2 weeks would take her to 43 weeks, with rising stillbirth risk. There is no indication for caesarean.
whyWrong: ARM is not possible through a closed cervix and risks cord prolapse with a high head.
Oxytocin on an unfavourable cervix often fails.
An unfavourable cervix is not an indication for caesarean.
Delaying to 43 weeks increases stillbirth risk.

quiz.stem:
A 29-year-old woman, G1P0, has been fully dilated for 2.5 hours with an epidural and has been actively pushing for 1.5 hours. The CTG shows early decelerations. On abdominal palpation, one-fifth of the head is palpable. Vaginal examination: fully dilated, membranes ruptured, vertex at station +1 in a direct occipito-anterior position with minimal caput. Her bladder was emptied 20 minutes ago. She is exhausted.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Allow a further 3 hours of pushing
Oxytocin infusion and review in 4 hours
Assisted vaginal birth with vacuum or forceps
quiz.explanation:
She has **delay in the second stage** with maternal exhaustion. All the prerequisites for **instrumental birth** are met: **fully dilated**, **membranes ruptured**, **position known** (occipito-anterior), head **engaged** (one-fifth palpable, station +1), **empty bladder**, effective **analgesia** (epidural). She should give consent and an experienced operator should perform it.

Vacuum causes less perineal trauma; forceps are more likely to succeed. A mediolateral episiotomy is usually recommended with forceps.

A caesarean with the head this low carries more morbidity (impacted head, extensions) and is not indicated when instrumental birth is feasible. Early decelerations are benign and do not require scalp sampling.
whyWrong: No immediate threat to life; the head is low and instrumental birth is feasible.
Prolonged pushing with exhaustion increases maternal and fetal morbidity.
Early decelerations reflect head compression and do not need scalp sampling.
A 4-hour wait is excessive in the second stage with exhaustion.

quiz.stem:
A 35-year-old woman, G4P3, is in spontaneous labour at 39 weeks. Her previous births were uncomplicated vaginal births of 3.4-3.6 kg babies. The cervix has remained at 7 cm for 4 hours despite regular strong contractions. There is marked caput and moulding, the head is 3/5 palpable, and she has haematuria on catheterisation. Pulse 108 bpm, temperature 37.8 °C.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: Epidural analgesia and review in 4 hours
quiz.explanation:
Secondary arrest of dilatation **despite strong contractions** in a **multiparous** woman, with **marked caput and moulding**, a **high head (3/5 palpable)**, **haematuria** and maternal tachycardia and fever, indicates **obstructed labour**. Possible causes include malposition, a larger baby this time, or a brow presentation.

The answer is **caesarean section**. **Oxytocin is dangerous** in obstructed labour, especially in a multiparous woman, because the uterus may **rupture**. Instrumental birth requires full dilatation and an engaged head. Waiting prolongs obstruction and risks rupture, fistula and sepsis.

**Rule:** in a multiparous woman, slow progress with strong contractions is obstruction until proven otherwise.
whyWrong: Oxytocin in obstructed labour risks uterine rupture, particularly in multiparas.
ARM does not overcome mechanical obstruction.
Delay risks rupture, fistula and sepsis.
Instrumental birth needs full dilatation and an engaged head.

lessons.title: Preterm labour, ruptured membranes and breech
objectives: Assess threatened preterm labour and use fetal fibronectin and cervical length appropriately
Give corticosteroids, tocolysis, magnesium neuroprotection and GBS prophylaxis correctly
Diagnose and manage prelabour rupture of membranes at term and preterm
Offer external cephalic version and counsel on mode of birth for breech

sections.heading: Why preterm birth matters
sections.body:
**Preterm birth** is birth before **37 weeks**. It occurs in about 8-9% of births in Australia and is higher among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women. It is the leading cause of neonatal death and long-term disability (cerebral palsy, chronic lung disease, developmental problems). Risk falls steeply with each additional week in utero, so buying time for steroids and transfer is valuable.

**Risk factors**: **previous spontaneous preterm birth** (the strongest), **short cervix** on ultrasound, cervical surgery (LLETZ, cone biopsy), multiple pregnancy, uterine anomalies, APH, infection (including chorioamnionitis and possibly bacterial vaginosis and UTI), polyhydramnios, smoking, young maternal age and socioeconomic disadvantage.

**Prevention**: women with a **short cervix** in the second trimester are offered **vaginal progesterone**; selected women with a history of preterm birth or cervical insufficiency receive a **cervical cerclage**. Smoking cessation helps. The Australian Preterm Birth Prevention Alliance promotes these measures.

sections.heading: Threatened preterm labour: assessment
sections.body:
Symptoms: regular tightenings, period-like pain, backache, pelvic pressure, show or increased discharge, or ruptured membranes. Many women with symptoms do not deliver soon; the challenge is to identify who will.

**Assessment**:

- History, observations (temperature and pulse for infection), abdominal palpation, CTG.
- **Sterile speculum examination**: cervical dilatation, bleeding, pooling of liquor, and swabs (high vaginal for GBS and infection).
- **Fetal fibronectin (fFN)**: a glycoprotein that "glues" the membranes to the decidua. A **negative test** has a very high negative predictive value: the woman is very unlikely to deliver within the next 7-14 days, which avoids unnecessary admission, transfer and steroids. Take the swab **before** a digital examination, and note that intercourse, bleeding and lubricant affect it.
- **Transvaginal cervical length**: a long cervix (for example 30 mm or more) is reassuring.
- Urine culture, and look for a cause (abruption, infection, polyhydramnios).

Avoid digital vaginal examination if membranes may have ruptured, because it introduces infection.

sections.heading: Managing preterm labour
sections.body:
If preterm labour is likely:

- **Corticosteroids**: **betamethasone** two doses 24 hours apart, for women at risk of birth within 7 days between about **24 and 34+6 weeks** (and from about 22-23 weeks in selected cases after counselling). They reduce neonatal death, respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis. Maximum benefit is from 24 hours to 7 days after the first dose.
- **Tocolysis**: to delay birth by about **48 hours** to complete steroids and allow **in-utero transfer** to a hospital with an appropriate neonatal unit. **Nifedipine** is commonly used in Australia; alternatives include atosiban and, before 32 weeks, indomethacin. Tocolysis does not improve neonatal outcome by itself. **Contraindications**: chorioamnionitis, significant APH or abruption, fetal compromise, lethal anomaly, and advanced labour. Nifedipine causes hypotension and headache.
- **Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection** when birth is imminent before **30 weeks** (Australian guideline), reducing cerebral palsy.
- **GBS prophylaxis**: **IV benzylpenicillin** in preterm labour, since GBS status is often unknown.
- **In-utero transfer** to a tertiary centre is safer than transferring a preterm newborn.

After 34+6 weeks, steroids are not routinely given (they may be considered before a planned caesarean before 39 weeks in some units), and tocolysis is not used.

sections.heading: Prelabour rupture of membranes
sections.body:
**Diagnosis**: history of a gush or continuous trickle, then **sterile speculum examination** showing **pooling** of fluid in the posterior fornix (ask her to cough). If unclear, a bedside test for amniotic fluid proteins (e.g. PAMG-1) helps. Ultrasound may show reduced liquor. **No digital examination** in preterm ROM unless she is in labour.

**Term PROM (37 weeks or more)**: about 60% labour within 24 hours. Offer **induction** or **expectant management for up to about 24 hours**. Induce promptly if **GBS positive** (with IV antibiotics), if there is meconium, any sign of infection, or if she prefers. Monitor temperature and fetal movements, and avoid intercourse and baths.

**Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM)** before 37 weeks:

- Admit. Look for chorioamnionitis (maternal fever and tachycardia, fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor, rising CRP or WCC).
- **Erythromycin** for up to 10 days, which prolongs pregnancy and reduces neonatal morbidity. **Amoxicillin-clavulanate is avoided** because it was associated with necrotising enterocolitis in the ORACLE trial.
- **Corticosteroids** if before 34+6 weeks, **magnesium** if birth is imminent before 30 weeks.
- In the absence of infection or other problems, expectant management until about **37 weeks** is reasonable (the Australian-led PPROMT trial supported this).
- **Deliver** if chorioamnionitis, abruption or fetal compromise develops, with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics.
- Before viability, PPROM carries risks of pulmonary hypoplasia and limb contractures; counselling is complex.

sections.heading: Breech and other malpresentations
sections.body:
**Breech** occurs in about 3-4% of term pregnancies (much more common preterm). Types: frank (extended legs), complete (flexed), footling. Associations: prematurity, uterine anomalies, fibroids, placenta praevia, polyhydramnios, fetal anomalies. Always check with ultrasound for placental site and anomalies.

**External cephalic version (ECV)**: offered from about **36-37 weeks**; successful in about half. It reduces caesarean rates. Performed in hospital with a CTG before and after, often with tocolysis. **Contraindications**: APH, placenta praevia, abnormal CTG, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy (except for the second twin after the first birth), major uterine anomaly, and another indication for caesarean. A previous caesarean is a relative contraindication. **Anti-D** for Rh D-negative women.

If ECV fails or is declined: **planned caesarean section** reduces perinatal morbidity compared with planned vaginal breech birth (Term Breech Trial), and is the most common choice. **Planned vaginal breech birth** is an option for selected women in units with experienced clinicians.

**Transverse or unstable lie** near term: risk of cord prolapse and arm prolapse when membranes rupture; admission may be advised from about 37 weeks, with ECV, stabilising induction or caesarean.

**Face presentation**: mentoanterior can deliver vaginally; mentoposterior cannot. **Brow**: the largest diameter (mentovertical), usually needs caesarean.

sections.heading: Traps and discriminating clues
sections.body:
- Symptoms at 30 weeks with a **negative fFN**: low risk of birth within 7-14 days; avoid unnecessary steroids and transfer.
- Steroid window: up to **34+6 weeks**.
- Magnesium neuroprotection: imminent birth **before 30 weeks**.
- PPROM antibiotic: **erythromycin**, not amoxicillin-clavulanate.
- Suspected ruptured membranes: **sterile speculum**, not digital examination.
- Tocolysis is wrong with chorioamnionitis or abruption.
- Breech at 37 weeks with no contraindications: offer **ECV**.

keyPoints: Preterm birth is before 37 weeks; the strongest risk factor is previous spontaneous preterm birth.
A negative fetal fibronectin makes birth within 7-14 days very unlikely.
Betamethasone two doses 24 hours apart from about 24 to 34+6 weeks.
Tocolysis (nifedipine) buys about 48 hours for steroids and in-utero transfer; contraindicated with infection or abruption.
Magnesium for fetal neuroprotection if birth is imminent before 30 weeks; IV benzylpenicillin for GBS.
PPROM: erythromycin, steroids, watch for chorioamnionitis, deliver around 37 weeks if well.
Breech at term: offer ECV from about 36-37 weeks; if it fails, planned caesarean is the usual choice.
redFlags: Maternal fever, tachycardia, uterine tenderness or fetal tachycardia after ruptured membranes
Bleeding with preterm contractions (abruption)
Cord or limb visible or felt after membrane rupture with malpresentation
Preterm labour in a hospital without a suitable neonatal unit (arrange in-utero transfer)

contrast.india: Ampicillin and amoxicillin-clavulanate combinations are commonly used.
contrast.australia: Erythromycin for up to 10 days; amoxicillin-clavulanate avoided because of NEC risk.

contrast.india: Used variably, often only for eclampsia.
contrast.australia: Recommended when birth is imminent before 30 weeks (Australian national guideline).

contrast.india: Vaginal breech birth is still performed in many centres, and ECV is less often offered.
contrast.australia: ECV offered routinely; planned caesarean if ECV fails, vaginal breech only in selected units.

quiz.stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 29+2 weeks' gestation presents to a regional hospital with regular painful contractions every 5 minutes. Speculum examination shows intact membranes and a cervix dilated 3 cm. She is afebrile and the CTG is normal. The regional hospital has a special care nursery that accepts babies from 32 weeks.

In addition to arranging in-utero transfer, which combination is most appropriate?
options: Magnesium sulfate for 24 hours, then discharge
Betamethasone, nifedipine, magnesium sulfate if birth is imminent, and IV benzylpenicillin
quiz.explanation:
She is in **established preterm labour at 29 weeks** (regular contractions with cervical change). Management:

- **Betamethasone** to reduce neonatal respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and death.
- **Tocolysis with nifedipine** to delay birth about 48 hours for steroids and **in-utero transfer** to a hospital with a NICU, since the local nursery only takes babies from 32 weeks.
- **Magnesium sulfate** for **fetal neuroprotection** if birth is imminent before 30 weeks.
- **IV benzylpenicillin** for GBS prophylaxis, as her status is unknown.

Erythromycin is for PPROM, which she does not have. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is associated with NEC.
whyWrong: Incomplete: she also needs tocolysis for transfer, neuroprotection and GBS prophylaxis.
Erythromycin is for ruptured membranes; her membranes are intact, and steroids are missing.
Magnesium alone omits steroids, and discharge is unsafe in established labour.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is associated with NEC and is not indicated.

quiz.stem:
A 31-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation reports a gush of clear fluid from the vagina 3 hours ago, with continued dampness. She has no contractions. Temperature 36.8 °C, pulse 80 bpm. CTG is normal. Sterile speculum examination shows a pool of clear fluid in the posterior vaginal fornix.

Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix
quiz.explanation:
Pooling of fluid on sterile speculum at 32 weeks confirms **preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM)**. She has no signs of infection or labour.

Management: **admit**, give **betamethasone** (she is under 34+6 weeks), and start **erythromycin** for up to 10 days, which prolongs the latency period and reduces neonatal morbidity. Monitor closely for **chorioamnionitis**. Without complications, expectant management to about 37 weeks is reasonable.

Avoid **digital examination**, which increases infection risk. **Amoxicillin-clavulanate** is avoided (NEC). Tocolysis is not recommended in PPROM without labour, and prolonged tocolysis has no benefit. Immediate induction at 32 weeks without infection increases prematurity complications.
whyWrong: Digital examination increases the risk of ascending infection.
Birth at 32 weeks without infection or other indication adds prematurity risks.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is linked with NEC, and she needs admission.
Tocolysis is not indicated without labour, and 7-day tocolysis has no benefit.

quiz.stem:
A 29-year-old woman, G1P0, at 37 weeks' gestation has a breech presentation confirmed on ultrasound. The placenta is fundal, liquor volume is normal and the fetus is appropriately grown with no anomalies. She is Rh D negative. She would prefer a vaginal birth if possible.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Book a caesarean section at 39 weeks without further discussion
Offer external cephalic version with anti-D afterwards
Reassess at 40 weeks as the baby may turn
Advise planned vaginal breech birth as first choice
quiz.explanation:
A breech presentation at 37 weeks in an uncomplicated pregnancy should be offered **external cephalic version (ECV)**. It succeeds in about half of cases and reduces the chance of caesarean section. She has no contraindications (no APH, placenta not praevia, normal liquor, normal CTG expected, singleton).

As she is **Rh D negative**, ECV is a sensitising event, so she needs **anti-D** with a Kleihauer test.

If ECV fails or she declines, options are a **planned caesarean at 39 weeks**, which lowers perinatal morbidity, or a planned vaginal breech birth in a unit with experienced clinicians after counselling. Spontaneous version becomes unlikely at term, so waiting is not useful.
whyWrong: Caesarean without offering ECV denies her the chance of a cephalic vaginal birth.
Inducing a breech is not the first step when ECV has not been tried.
Spontaneous version at term is uncommon; delay loses the ECV window.
Vaginal breech is for selected women after ECV is declined or fails, in experienced units.

lessons.title: Intrapartum fetal surveillance and CTG
objectives: Choose between intermittent auscultation and continuous CTG
Read a CTG systematically: baseline, variability, accelerations and decelerations
Explain the physiology behind early, variable and late decelerations
Respond to an abnormal CTG with conservative measures, scalp sampling or expedited birth

sections.heading: The guideline and its purpose
sections.body:
Fetal surveillance in labour aims to identify a fetus developing **hypoxia** in time to act, while avoiding unnecessary intervention in the many fetuses who are coping. The Australian reference is the **RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance (IFS) Clinical Guideline**, and most clinicians complete the RANZCOG **FSEP** education program.

**Intermittent auscultation** is appropriate for low-risk women in spontaneous labour. **Continuous CTG** is recommended when there are risk factors, for example:

- **Maternal**: previous caesarean, pre-eclampsia or hypertension, diabetes on medication, APH, prolonged rupture of membranes, **maternal fever** or suspected infection, significant medical disease.
- **Fetal**: growth restriction, preterm labour, multiple pregnancy, breech, reduced fetal movements, oligohydramnios, abnormal Dopplers.
- **Intrapartum**: **oxytocin** use, **epidural**, significant meconium, abnormal auscultation, prolonged labour, vaginal bleeding.

CTG in low-risk women increases caesarean and instrumental birth without improving outcomes other than a small reduction in neonatal seizures.

sections.heading: Reading the CTG: the features
sections.body:
A systematic approach (many use **DR C BRAVADO**: Define Risk, Contractions, Baseline RAte, Variability, Accelerations, Decelerations, Overall) keeps you from missing features. RANZCOG defines:

| Feature | Normal | Abnormal |
|---|---|---|
| **Baseline rate** | **110-160 bpm** | Tachycardia above 160; bradycardia below 110 (below 100 is more concerning) |
| **Variability** | **6-25 bpm** | Reduced (3-5), absent (less than 3), increased (more than 25) |
| **Accelerations** | Present (rises of 15 bpm for 15 s) are reassuring | Absence in labour on its own is of uncertain significance |
| **Decelerations** | None or early | Variable, late, prolonged |
| **Contractions** | Up to about 5 in 10 minutes | Tachysystole: more than 5 in 10 minutes |

**Causes of baseline tachycardia**: maternal fever and **chorioamnionitis**, fetal hypoxia (a rising baseline is a sign of a stressed fetus), maternal tachycardia, dehydration, drugs (terbutaline), fetal anaemia, prematurity.

**Reduced variability**: fetal sleep (usually under 40 minutes), opioids, magnesium, prematurity, or **hypoxia**. Variability reflects an intact, well-oxygenated autonomic nervous system; losing it is a key warning sign.

**Sinusoidal pattern**: smooth regular sine wave with absent variability, associated with severe **fetal anaemia** (feto-maternal haemorrhage, vasa praevia, alloimmunisation) or severe hypoxia.

sections.heading: The physiology of decelerations
sections.body:
- **Early decelerations**: gradual, symmetrical, mirror the contraction (nadir at the peak). Caused by **head compression** triggering a vagal reflex. **Benign.** Common in late first and second stage.
- **Variable decelerations**: abrupt drop and recovery, varying in shape, size and timing. Caused by **cord compression**. Often with "shoulders" (brief accelerations before and after). Concerning features ("complicated variables") include long duration (over 60 seconds), deep drops, slow recovery, loss of variability within the deceleration, and a rising baseline.
- **Late decelerations**: gradual, start after the contraction begins, nadir after the peak, and recover after the contraction has ended. Caused by **uteroplacental insufficiency**: during each contraction, placental blood flow falls, the fetus becomes hypoxic, and chemoreceptors trigger the response. **Recurrent late decelerations are concerning**, especially with reduced variability or tachycardia.
- **Prolonged deceleration**: a sustained fall lasting minutes. Causes include cord prolapse, abruption, uterine rupture, tachysystole, maternal hypotension (after an epidural top-up or supine position) and rapid descent. A prolonged deceleration of around 3 minutes or more that is not recovering needs immediate action and preparation for urgent birth.

**Big picture**: a fetus compensating for hypoxia first shows decelerations, then a **rising baseline** and loss of accelerations, then **reduced variability**. Tachycardia with reduced variability and recurrent decelerations is a very worrying combination.

sections.heading: Responding to an abnormal CTG
sections.body:
**1. Look for and reverse the cause** (intrauterine resuscitation):

- **Change maternal position** to the left or right lateral (relieves aortocaval and cord compression).
- **Stop or reduce oxytocin**; consider **tocolysis** (e.g. terbutaline) for tachysystole.
- **IV fluids** and treat hypotension (e.g. after epidural).
- **Check the maternal pulse** to be sure the CTG is not recording the mother's heart rate.
- **Vaginal examination** to exclude cord prolapse and assess progress.
- Treat maternal fever (paracetamol) and consider infection.

**2. If the abnormality persists but birth is not immediately needed**, **fetal scalp blood sampling** (FBS) can clarify fetal acid-base status:

| Test | Normal | Borderline | Abnormal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scalp lactate (mmol/L) | Below 4.2 | 4.2-4.8 | Above 4.8 |
| Scalp pH | 7.25 or more | 7.20-7.24 | Below 7.20 |

An abnormal result means **expedite birth**. Borderline results need repeat sampling or reassessment. FBS is **contraindicated** with maternal blood-borne virus infection (HIV, hepatitis B or C), fetal bleeding disorders, prematurity (under about 34 weeks) and face presentation, and it is not used when the CTG is clearly pre-terminal.

**3. Expedite birth** by the fastest safe route (instrumental if fully dilated and suitable, otherwise caesarean, category 1 or 2) when the CTG suggests likely hypoxia and conservative measures fail, or with a prolonged unrecovering bradycardia.

**After birth**: take **paired cord blood gases** (arterial and venous) when there were CTG concerns, an operative birth for fetal compromise or a low Apgar score. Arterial pH and base excess or lactate document the fetal condition at birth. Document the CTG review and decisions carefully.

sections.heading: Traps and discriminating clues
sections.body:
- Early decelerations in the second stage: **normal**; continue.
- Variable decelerations with normal baseline and variability: **cord compression**, change position; not an emergency by itself.
- Recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability: likely hypoxia; if not fully dilated, prepare for **caesarean** or FBS if time allows.
- Baseline 170 bpm with a maternal temperature of 38.5 °C: think **chorioamnionitis**.
- Sudden prolonged bradycardia after epidural top-up: **maternal hypotension**; left lateral, fluids, vasopressor.
- Sinusoidal trace: **fetal anaemia** (vasa praevia, feto-maternal haemorrhage).
- FBS in an HIV-positive or hepatitis B-positive woman is contraindicated.

keyPoints: Low-risk labour: intermittent auscultation; risk factors, oxytocin, epidural or fever: continuous CTG.
Normal CTG: baseline 110-160 bpm, variability 6-25 bpm, accelerations, no decelerations other than early.
Early decelerations mean head compression (benign); variable mean cord compression; late mean uteroplacental insufficiency.
Reduced variability, rising baseline and recurrent late decelerations together suggest hypoxia.
First respond with position change, stopping oxytocin, fluids and checking the maternal pulse.
Scalp lactate above 4.8 mmol/L or pH below 7.20 means expedite birth.
Take paired cord gases after a concerning labour or a low Apgar.
redFlags: Prolonged deceleration or bradycardia that does not recover
Recurrent late decelerations with reduced or absent variability
Sinusoidal pattern
Rising baseline with maternal fever

contrast.india: Classification systems vary between institutions; NICE or FIGO categories are often taught.
contrast.australia: RANZCOG IFS guideline and the FSEP education program are standard across Australian units.

contrast.india: Fetal scalp blood sampling is rarely available.
contrast.australia: Scalp lactate (and pH) are used in many Australian units to clarify an abnormal CTG.

quiz.stem:
A 28-year-old primigravida is in labour at 40 weeks on an oxytocin infusion for slow progress. The cervix is 6 cm. The CTG over the last 40 minutes shows a baseline of 165 bpm, variability of 3-4 bpm, and decelerations that begin after the peak of each contraction and return to baseline 30 seconds after the contraction ends. Contractions are 6 in 10 minutes. Maternal temperature is 37.2 °C.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Stop the oxytocin, reposition the woman to her side and give IV fluids
Increase the oxytocin to speed up labour
Give an epidural to relax the uterus
quiz.explanation:
The CTG shows **recurrent late decelerations**, **reduced variability** and a **rising baseline**, in the setting of **tachysystole** (6 contractions in 10 minutes) from oxytocin. Excessive contractions reduce placental perfusion, causing hypoxia.

The immediate response is **intrauterine resuscitation**: **stop the oxytocin**, move her to the **lateral position**, give **IV fluids**, check the maternal pulse, and consider **tocolysis** (terbutaline) if tachysystole persists. Call for senior review.

If the CTG does not improve quickly, she needs **fetal scalp sampling** if appropriate, or **expedited birth**, which at 6 cm means caesarean section.

Increasing oxytocin would worsen hypoxia.
whyWrong: More oxytocin worsens tachysystole and hypoxia.
These features suggest possible hypoxia and need action now.
ARM does not treat tachysystole or late decelerations.
An epidural does not correct tachysystole and may cause hypotension.

quiz.stem:
A 30-year-old woman, G2P1, is in the second stage of labour with continuous CTG because of an epidural. The baseline is 135 bpm with variability of 10 bpm. With each contraction there is a gradual, symmetrical fall in heart rate of about 20 bpm that reaches its lowest point at the peak of the contraction and recovers as the contraction ends.

What is the most likely cause of these decelerations?
quiz.explanation:
Gradual, symmetrical decelerations that **mirror the contraction** (lowest point at the peak, recovery as it ends) are **early decelerations**. They result from **fetal head compression** during contractions, which increases intracranial pressure and triggers a vagal reflex.

They are **benign**, particularly in the late first and second stage, and do not need intervention when baseline and variability are normal, as here.

Late decelerations (uteroplacental insufficiency) start and recover after the contraction. Variable decelerations (cord compression) are abrupt and variable in shape and timing. Fetal anaemia gives a sinusoidal pattern. Maternal hypotension usually causes a prolonged deceleration.
whyWrong: Uteroplacental insufficiency causes late decelerations, which lag behind the contraction.
Cord compression causes abrupt variable decelerations.
Fetal anaemia typically produces a sinusoidal trace.
Maternal hypotension causes a prolonged deceleration, not a repeating mirror pattern.

quiz.stem:
A 33-year-old woman at 39 weeks is in labour, 7 cm dilated. The CTG has shown a baseline of 150 bpm with reduced variability and recurrent variable decelerations lasting 60-70 seconds for 30 minutes. Position change and stopping oxytocin have not improved the trace. Her booking bloods showed she is hepatitis B surface antigen positive. The obstetric registrar is considering fetal scalp blood sampling.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Fetal scalp electrode and continue observation for 2 hours
quiz.explanation:
The CTG shows **complicated variable decelerations** (long, recurrent) with **reduced variability**, persisting despite intrauterine resuscitation. This raises concern for fetal hypoxia.

Fetal scalp blood sampling would normally be an option to clarify fetal acid-base status when birth is not immediately required. However, it is **contraindicated in women with blood-borne viruses** (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV) because it breaches the fetal skin and increases the risk of vertical transmission. A scalp electrode carries the same concern.

With an abnormal, non-improving CTG and no way to clarify, the next step is to **expedite birth**. At 7 cm, that means **caesarean section**. Instrumental birth requires full dilatation.
whyWrong: Scalp sampling is contraindicated in maternal hepatitis B.
Scalp electrodes are also avoided with blood-borne viruses, and observation is unsafe.
Instrumental birth requires full dilatation; she is 7 cm.
Tocolysis is for tachysystole; oxytocin has already been stopped and the trace remains abnormal.
quiz.ausPearl: The RANZCOG IFS guideline lists maternal blood-borne viral infection as a contraindication to fetal blood sampling.

lessons.title: Perineal trauma and the puerperium
objectives: Classify perineal tears and describe the management of anal sphincter injuries
Describe normal postpartum physiology: involution, lochia and recovery
Work through fever and other complications in the postpartum period
Conduct a thorough six-week postnatal check

sections.heading: Why the perineum matters
sections.body:
Most women who have a vaginal birth sustain some perineal trauma. **Obstetric anal sphincter injuries (OASIS)**, third and fourth degree tears, occur in about 3-5% of first vaginal births in Australia and are a major cause of **anal incontinence** in women. Rates are higher in women of **South Asian** background, which is relevant for Indian students to know. Australian maternity services have adopted a national **perineal protection bundle** to reduce OASIS.

The **puerperium** is the 6 weeks after birth, when the body returns to its non-pregnant state. It carries risks of haemorrhage, infection, VTE, pre-eclampsia and mental illness.

sections.heading: Classification of perineal tears
sections.body:
| Degree | Structures involved |
|---|---|
| First | Perineal skin and/or vaginal mucosa only |
| Second | Perineal muscles (not the anal sphincter) |
| **Third 3a** | Less than 50% of the **external anal sphincter (EAS)** thickness |
| **Third 3b** | More than 50% of the EAS |
| **Third 3c** | EAS and **internal anal sphincter (IAS)** |
| **Fourth** | Sphincter complex and the **anal or rectal mucosa** |

**Risk factors for OASIS**: first vaginal birth, **forceps** (more than vacuum), birthweight over 4 kg, persistent **occipito-posterior** position, prolonged second stage, shoulder dystocia, midline episiotomy, and Asian ethnicity.

**Prevention**: warm perineal compresses in the second stage, slow controlled birth of the head with hands-on perineal support, and a **mediolateral episiotomy** (angled about 60 degrees from the midline at crowning) for instrumental births, especially forceps.

**Every woman should have a rectal examination** after a vaginal birth with perineal trauma, and again after repair, to detect sphincter injury and exclude sutures through the rectal mucosa.

sections.heading: Repair and follow-up of OASIS
sections.body:
- **Repair in theatre** by an experienced clinician, under regional or general anaesthesia with good light, using recognised techniques (overlapping or end-to-end repair of the EAS, separate repair of the IAS).
- **Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics** at repair (and often a short oral course) to reduce infection and wound breakdown.
- **Laxatives** (stool softeners) for about 10 days to avoid straining and hard stools; avoid constipating codeine.
- Analgesia: paracetamol and NSAIDs; ice packs.
- **Pelvic floor physiotherapy** before discharge.
- **Review at about 6-12 weeks** in a perineal clinic: ask about **faecal urgency and incontinence of flatus or stool**, dyspareunia and wound healing. Refer for endoanal ultrasound and anorectal manometry if symptomatic.
- **Future births**: women without ongoing symptoms and with normal testing can usually plan a vaginal birth; women with persistent symptoms or abnormal studies should be offered a caesarean section.

A missed or poorly repaired sphincter injury can lead to lifelong incontinence and **rectovaginal fistula**.

**Perineal haematoma** presents with severe perineal pain and a tense swelling, sometimes with shock; it may need drainage in theatre.

**Postpartum urinary retention** is common after epidural and instrumental birth. Women should void within about 6 hours of birth (or catheter removal); measure volumes and catheterise if retaining, to prevent long-term bladder damage.

sections.heading: Normal puerperal physiology
sections.body:
- **Uterus**: at the umbilicus after birth, shrinking by about a finger's breadth a day, and no longer palpable abdominally by about 10-14 days. "After pains" occur with breastfeeding (oxytocin).
- **Lochia**: red (rubra) for the first few days, then pink-brown (serosa), then yellow-white (alba), lasting up to about 4-6 weeks. Heavy fresh bleeding, clots or an offensive smell are abnormal.
- **Cardiovascular**: blood volume and cardiac output return to normal over weeks; **VTE risk is highest in the first 6 weeks**, especially after caesarean section.
- **Ovulation** can return from about 3-4 weeks in women who are not breastfeeding.
- **Thyroid**: **postpartum thyroiditis** (a hyperthyroid phase then a hypothyroid phase) affects some women in the first year, particularly those with thyroid antibodies, and can mimic depression.
- **Sheehan syndrome**: pituitary necrosis after severe PPH, presenting with **failure of lactation**, fatigue and later hypopituitarism.

sections.heading: Postpartum fever and complications
sections.body:
Fever of **38 °C or more** after birth needs a systematic search:

| Source | Clues | First management |
|---|---|---|
| **Endometritis** (womb) | Uterine tenderness, offensive lochia, bleeding, often after caesarean or prolonged labour | Swabs, cultures; antibiotics per Therapeutic Guidelines (oral amoxicillin-clavulanate if mild; IV broad-spectrum if unwell); ultrasound for retained products |
| **Mastitis** (breast) | Wedge-shaped, red, tender area, flu-like, usually from about week 1-6 | Continue breastfeeding; flucloxacillin or dicloxacillin if not settling or systemically unwell |
| **UTI or pyelonephritis** (water) | Dysuria, loin pain; catheterised in labour | MSU and antibiotics |
| **Wound infection** | Caesarean or perineal wound red, discharging | Swab, antibiotics, drain collections |
| **VTE** (walking) | Calf swelling, pleuritic pain, breathlessness, tachycardia | Imaging and LMWH |
| Chest (wind) | Cough, reduced air entry after general anaesthetic | CXR, physiotherapy, antibiotics if pneumonia |

**Group A streptococcal sepsis** can progress rapidly; a woman with fever, tachycardia, severe pain or diarrhoea and vomiting needs urgent review and IV antibiotics.

**Postpartum pre-eclampsia** can present up to several weeks after birth, most often in the first week: headache, visual symptoms, high BP. Check BP in any postpartum woman with a headache.

sections.heading: The six-week postnatal check
sections.body:
Usually done by the GP (often with the baby's check). Cover:

- **Mood**: EPDS, sleep, support, family violence (ask privately).
- **Physical recovery**: bleeding, perineum or caesarean wound, **continence** (urinary and faecal), pelvic floor exercises, dyspareunia and resuming sex.
- **BP** and follow-up of pregnancy complications: **75 g OGTT** if she had GDM, BP review and urine if she had pre-eclampsia (and her long-term cardiovascular risk), anaemia.
- **Contraception**.
- **Breastfeeding** and infant feeding concerns.
- **Vaccinations**: MMR if rubella non-immune (if not given in hospital), and catch-up for others.
- **Cervical screening** if due (can usually be done from 6 weeks).
- Plans for future pregnancy: interpregnancy interval, folic acid, and what to expect next time (e.g. after OASIS, caesarean or pre-eclampsia).

sections.heading: Traps and discriminating clues
sections.body:
- Tear involving more than half of the external sphincter: **3b**; internal sphincter too: **3c**; anal mucosa: **fourth degree**.
- OASIS: repair **in theatre**, antibiotics, laxatives, physiotherapy and follow-up.
- Faecal urgency months after a forceps birth: suspect an unrecognised sphincter injury; **endoanal ultrasound**.
- Postpartum headache with high BP: **postpartum pre-eclampsia**.
- Postpartum woman who cannot breastfeed after massive PPH: **Sheehan syndrome**.
- Fever day 3 after caesarean with uterine tenderness and offensive lochia: **endometritis**.

keyPoints: Third degree tears: 3a less than 50% EAS, 3b more than 50%, 3c includes IAS; fourth degree includes anal mucosa.
Rectal examination after every vaginal birth with perineal trauma.
OASIS: repair in theatre, antibiotics, laxatives, physiotherapy and review at 6-12 weeks.
Mediolateral episiotomy with forceps reduces OASIS.
Postpartum fever sources: womb, breast, urine, wound, legs and chest.
Postpartum pre-eclampsia can present weeks after birth; check BP with any headache.
Six-week check: mood, contraception, continence, BP, OGTT after GDM, vaccines and cervical screening.
redFlags: Fever with tachycardia, severe pain, vomiting or diarrhoea postpartum (GAS sepsis)
Heavy fresh bleeding or offensive lochia (secondary PPH, endometritis)
Postpartum headache with raised BP
Faecal incontinence or passage of stool or flatus per vagina
Unilateral leg swelling or breathlessness

contrast.india: Family-supported confinement period; ASHA home visits in rural areas.
contrast.australia: Midwife home visits, maternal and child health nurse, and GP check at 6 weeks.

contrast.india: Rectal examination after birth is not always done.

quiz.stem:
A 27-year-old primigravida has a forceps birth of a 4.1 kg baby. On examination, including a rectal examination, there is a tear through the perineal muscles involving about two-thirds of the thickness of the external anal sphincter. The internal anal sphincter and anal mucosa are intact.

How should this tear be classified?
quiz.explanation:
Perineal tears are classified by the deepest structure involved. Injury to **more than 50% of the external anal sphincter** thickness, with the internal sphincter intact, is a **3b** tear.

- 3a: less than 50% of the EAS.
- 3c: both EAS and IAS.
- Fourth degree: the sphincter complex plus the anal or rectal mucosa.

She has several risk factors: first vaginal birth, forceps and a baby over 4 kg.

Management: repair **in theatre** by an experienced clinician, IV antibiotics, laxatives, analgesia, pelvic floor physiotherapy, and follow-up at 6-12 weeks for continence symptoms.
whyWrong: Second degree tears do not involve the anal sphincter.
3a involves less than 50% of the EAS; here two-thirds is torn.
3c requires internal sphincter involvement, which is intact.
Fourth degree requires anal mucosal involvement.

quiz.stem:
A 31-year-old woman is on day 4 after an emergency caesarean section for failure to progress after 20 hours of labour with ruptured membranes. She has a temperature of 38.7 °C, pulse 110 bpm and lower abdominal pain. The uterus is tender and the lochia is offensive. The wound looks clean. Her breasts are soft and non-tender and calves are normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.explanation:
Fever, **uterine tenderness** and **offensive lochia** a few days after birth indicate **endometritis**. **Caesarean section after prolonged labour with ruptured membranes** is the strongest risk factor, because vaginal organisms ascend and the uterine incision provides a nidus.

Management: blood cultures, high vaginal swab, FBC and CRP; **broad-spectrum antibiotics** per Therapeutic Guidelines (IV when systemically unwell, as here, covering streptococci, Gram-negatives and anaerobes); pelvic ultrasound for retained products or collection if not settling. Consider **group A streptococcus** if she deteriorates rapidly.

The clean wound, soft breasts and normal calves make the other options less likely.
whyWrong: The wound is clean; the uterine findings point to the endometrium.
Her breasts are soft and non-tender.
PE does not cause offensive lochia or uterine tenderness.
No urinary symptoms or loin pain; the uterine findings point elsewhere.

quiz.stem:
A 30-year-old woman presents to her GP 9 days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth with a severe headache for 12 hours and blurred vision. She had normal BP throughout pregnancy. BP is 172/108 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows 2+ protein. She is breastfeeding.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral paracetamol and review in 2 days
Advise stopping breastfeeding and start an ACE inhibitor
Start oral methyldopa and review in 1 week
Urgent transfer to hospital for antihypertensive therapy and magnesium sulfate
quiz.explanation:
Pre-eclampsia can present for the first time **after birth**, usually in the first week but sometimes later, and eclampsia can occur postpartum. She has **severe hypertension** (160/110 or more), **neurological symptoms** (headache, visual disturbance) and proteinuria: **postpartum pre-eclampsia with severe features**.

She needs **urgent hospital transfer** for **acute BP control** and **magnesium sulfate** for seizure prophylaxis, with bloods (FBC, LFTs, creatinine) and neurological assessment. Imaging is considered for atypical features, to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, stroke or PRES.

Breastfeeding can continue: nifedipine, labetalol and enalapril are compatible. Methyldopa is avoided postpartum because of depression, and is too slow for severe hypertension.
whyWrong: This misses a potentially life-threatening condition.
Breastfeeding does not need to stop; many antihypertensives are compatible.
Outpatient imaging delays urgent treatment of severe hypertension.
Methyldopa is slow, avoided postpartum, and she needs same-day care.

lessons.title: Breastfeeding and postpartum contraception
objectives: Support breastfeeding and recognise signs of adequate milk transfer
Diagnose and manage mastitis, breast abscess and nipple problems
Check whether a medicine is compatible with breastfeeding and name key exceptions
Choose safe postpartum contraception by timing and breastfeeding status

sections.heading: Why breastfeeding matters
sections.body:
The **NHMRC Infant Feeding Guidelines** recommend **exclusive breastfeeding until around 6 months**, then continued breastfeeding with appropriate solid foods until 12 months and beyond, for as long as mother and baby wish. Most Australian women start breastfeeding, but rates of exclusive breastfeeding fall sharply over the first months.

**Benefits for the baby**: fewer gastrointestinal, respiratory and ear infections, lower risk of SIDS, and possibly lower rates of obesity and diabetes. **For the mother**: lower risk of breast and ovarian cancer and type 2 diabetes, and lactational amenorrhoea.

The doctor's role: support, fix problems early, prescribe safely, and avoid unnecessarily telling women to stop.

sections.heading: Physiology and signs of adequate feeding
sections.body:
- **Prolactin** from the anterior pituitary drives **milk production**; it rises with suckling and at night.
- **Oxytocin** from the posterior pituitary causes the **let-down reflex** and uterine contraction ("after pains"). Stress and pain can inhibit it.
- **Colostrum** is produced in the first days: small volume, rich in immunoglobulins. Milk "comes in" (lactogenesis II) around **days 2-4**, triggered by the fall in progesterone after delivery of the placenta. Retained placental tissue can delay it.
- Supply follows demand: frequent, effective feeding (8-12 times in 24 hours in the early weeks) builds supply.

**Signs a baby is getting enough**: at least about 6 heavy wet nappies a day after the first week, regular yellow stools, a contented baby after feeds, and weight gain. Babies commonly lose up to about 7-10% of birth weight in the first days and should regain birth weight by about **2 weeks**. Greater loss or jaundice should prompt a feeding assessment.

**Good attachment**: wide open mouth, chin in the breast, more areola visible above than below, and no pain after the first few sucks. Poor attachment causes most nipple pain and damage, and reduced supply. Lactation consultants and child health nurses are key supports; also consider **tongue-tie** when attachment problems persist.

sections.heading: Breast problems
sections.body:
| Problem | Features | Management |
|---|---|---|
| **Engorgement** | Both breasts full, hard, warm, often days 3-5 | Frequent feeding, hand expression to soften the areola, cold packs, analgesia |
| **Blocked duct / inflammation** | Tender lump, no systemic features | Continue feeding, gentle lymphatic massage, anti-inflammatories, ice; avoid deep massage |
| **Mastitis** | Wedge-shaped red, hot, tender area; fever, flu-like symptoms | **Continue breastfeeding** or expressing from the affected side; analgesia (paracetamol, ibuprofen). Antibiotics if not improving within 12-24 hours or if unwell: **flucloxacillin or dicloxacillin** (cefalexin for non-severe penicillin allergy; clindamycin for severe allergy or MRSA risk) per Therapeutic Guidelines |
| **Breast abscess** | Fluctuant, tender mass, persistent fever despite antibiotics | **Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration** (repeated if needed) or incision and drainage, plus antibiotics; breastfeeding can usually continue from the other side and often the affected side |
| **Nipple thrush** | Burning, shooting pain after feeds, shiny pink nipple, oral thrush in baby | Treat mother and baby with topical antifungal (e.g. miconazole) |

Stopping breastfeeding abruptly during mastitis increases the risk of abscess. A **persistent lump** after treatment needs imaging to exclude an abscess or, rarely, a breast cancer (including inflammatory carcinoma).

sections.heading: Medicines and breastfeeding
sections.body:
**Most medicines are compatible with breastfeeding.** The dose reaching the baby is usually a small fraction of the maternal dose. Before advising a woman to stop, check a reliable source: for example the Royal Women's Hospital *Pregnancy and Breastfeeding Medicines Guide*, state medicines information services, the Australian Medicines Handbook or LactMed.

**Generally compatible**: paracetamol, ibuprofen, most antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides), **sertraline** and most SSRIs, labetalol, nifedipine, **enalapril**, **warfarin**, **LMWH**, levothyroxine, insulin, metformin, prednisolone, most inhaled asthma medications, local anaesthetics, and most antiepileptics (with infant monitoring).

**Avoid or use with specialist advice**:

- **Codeine** and **tramadol**: codeine can cause serious opioid toxicity in breastfed babies of mothers who are ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolisers; the TGA advises against codeine in breastfeeding.
- **Lithium**: can accumulate in the infant; use only with specialist monitoring.
- Cytotoxic drugs, **radioactive iodine**, amiodarone, and some antithyroid drugs at high doses.
- **Combined oestrogen contraception** reduces milk supply in the early weeks.
- **DOACs**: limited data, generally avoided.

**Drugs affecting lactation**: domperidone and metoclopramide are sometimes used to increase supply; **cabergoline** is used to suppress lactation (e.g. after stillbirth), and bromocriptine is no longer recommended.

**Maternal conditions**: breastfeeding is recommended with **hepatitis B** (baby immunised at birth) and **hepatitis C** (consider pausing and expressing if nipples are cracked and bleeding). In Australia, women with **HIV** are generally advised to formula feed, although guidance is evolving for women with a sustained undetectable viral load, who should decide with specialist support. Active untreated TB needs treatment first. Infant **galactosaemia** is a contraindication.

sections.heading: Postpartum contraception
sections.body:
Ovulation can return from about **3-4 weeks** after birth in women who are not breastfeeding, often before the first period. Contraception should be discussed antenatally and in place **from 3 weeks** (day 21) if needed. Australia generally uses the **UK Medical Eligibility Criteria (UKMEC)**.

**Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM)**: about 98% effective if **all three** apply: fully or nearly fully breastfeeding (including at night), **amenorrhoeic**, and **less than 6 months** after birth.

| Method | When postpartum | Breastfeeding? |
|---|---|---|
| **Progestogen-only implant** | Any time (including immediately) | Safe |
| **Progestogen-only pill** (LNG, norethisterone, drospirenone) | Any time | Safe |
| **DMPA injection** | Any time (often from 6 weeks if breastfeeding in some protocols; check local guidance) | Safe |
| **Copper or LNG IUD** | **Within 48 hours** of birth, or **from 4 weeks** (higher expulsion and perforation risk between) | Safe |
| **Combined hormonal contraception** | **Not before 6 weeks if breastfeeding** (reduces supply; VTE). If not breastfeeding, **not before 21 days** (VTE risk), and with caution to 6 weeks if other VTE risk factors | Avoid in the first 6 weeks |
| Condoms, sterilisation, vasectomy | Any time | Safe |

**Progestogen-only methods are the default safe choice while breastfeeding.** Emergency contraception is not needed before day 21 postpartum.

**Interpregnancy interval**: short intervals (less than about 18 months from birth to conception) are associated with preterm birth and other adverse outcomes; after a caesarean, a short interval also increases the risk of uterine rupture in a subsequent labour.

sections.heading: Traps and discriminating clues
sections.body:
- Mastitis: **keep breastfeeding**; flucloxacillin or dicloxacillin if not settling.
- Persistent fluctuant mass despite antibiotics: **abscess**, ultrasound and aspiration.
- Breastfeeding woman at 3 weeks wanting the combined pill: **not yet**; offer a progestogen-only method.
- Breastfeeding woman needing analgesia: paracetamol and ibuprofen; **avoid codeine**.
- LAM needs all three criteria: exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, under 6 months.
- IUD insertion: within 48 hours or after 4 weeks.
- Warfarin and enalapril are compatible with breastfeeding.

keyPoints: Exclusive breastfeeding to around 6 months, continuing with solids to 12 months and beyond (NHMRC).
Babies should regain birth weight by about 2 weeks; poor attachment causes most nipple pain.
Mastitis: continue feeding; flucloxacillin or dicloxacillin if not improving in 12-24 hours or unwell.
Breast abscess: ultrasound-guided aspiration plus antibiotics.
Most drugs are compatible with breastfeeding; avoid codeine; check a reliable source first.
Progestogen-only methods are safe any time while breastfeeding; avoid combined methods in the first 6 weeks.
LAM works only if fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic and under 6 months.
redFlags: Breast lump that persists after treatment of mastitis (abscess or malignancy)
Baby with poor weight gain, few wet nappies or prolonged jaundice
Mother with mastitis who is systemically unwell or septic

contrast.australia: Midwives, lactation consultants, child health nurses and the Australian Breastfeeding Association; no prelacteal feeds.

contrast.australia: Implants, progestogen-only pills and IUDs are common first choices; combined methods delayed until 6 weeks if breastfeeding.
